questions.q: How does SOQL check whether a field has no value?
options: WHERE Field IS MISSING
WHERE Field IS NULL
WHERE Field = null
WHERE ISBLANK(Field)
questions.explain: SOQL has no IS NULL syntax at all; you compare directly against the null keyword with = or !=.

questions.q: How do you find records where a field DOES have a value in SOQL?
options: WHERE Field != null
WHERE Field IS NOT NULL
WHERE Field <> MISSING
WHERE NOT ISBLANK(Field)
questions.explain: != null is SOQL's form for 'has a value', the counterpart to = null for 'has no value'.

questions.q: A Contact with a blank AccountId is queried with SELECT Name, Account.Industry FROM Contact. What happens to that row?
options: Salesforce automatically substitutes a default Account record
It is silently excluded, the way an inner join would exclude it
The query throws a runtime error because the parent relationship is missing
It still comes back, with Account.Industry returned as null, rather than being excluded
questions.explain: Relationship queries behave like outer joins — a missing parent doesn't drop the child record, it just returns the referenced parent field as null.

questions.q: Per Salesforce's own documentation, why might you add a Field__c != null condition even when another condition in the same query already excludes blank values?
options: It is required syntax whenever a bind variable is used
It can help the query optimizer run the query more efficiently
It converts the query into an aggregate query
It prevents the query from counting as a SOQL query against governor limits
questions.explain: Salesforce's Apex documentation recommends explicitly excluding nulls in the WHERE clause specifically to improve query performance, even when another filter already rules out blanks.

questions.q: WHERE Email = null OR Phone = null AND Status = 'Open' (written without parentheses) is risky because:
options: Email and Phone cannot both be checked for null in the same query
SOQL does not allow combining a null check with AND
AND binds tighter than OR, so the clause may not group the conditions the way you intended
Status must always be the first condition in a WHERE clause
questions.explain: Without explicit parentheses, operator precedence evaluates AND before OR, which can silently change the intended meaning of a mixed condition.
